# Reviewer: Evidence audit of “Feynman as an AI-Eval-Quality Case Study”

**Reviewed artifact:** `outputs/feynman-eval-quality-case-study.md` (2026-11-14, 37,121 bytes)
**Review mode:** adversarial evidence audit — verify the case study’s claims against the local artifacts it cites, the upstream repository at the recorded SHA, and the external sources needed to check quoted release notes and adjacent-paper citations.
**Scope:** factual errors, misreadings of `evals/run.mjs`, unsupported quantitative claims, and overclaims. Novelty commentary is out of scope.

---

## Summary

The case study argues that Feynman’s verification stack is stronger than its evaluation stack: the bundled verifier catches planted claim-level defects, while the official `/lit` eval measures citation metadata and liveness rather than claim support. The strongest evidence is the `--rescore` blindspot probe: a synthetic `q01` output with a deliberately false claim and a real, resolving Snell et al. citation scores 100% on `done`, `valid`, `title`, and `recall`. That result is reproduced in `probes/eval-scorer-blindspot/row.jsonl`, and the scorer code confirms the metric definitions that make it possible.

The case study’s audit of the committed eval results is also largely accurate: the arithmetic (22 rows, 18 completed, 137,664,710 tokens, 20,591 wall seconds, `cost_usd = 0`) matches `official-eval/summary.md`; the published `npm test`/`architecture:check` failures are real; and the telemetry error-path leak reproduces against both 0.5.65 and 0.5.69. But four claims presented as verified need correction: the “24/24” provenance overstates what `aggregate.py` computes, the researcher probe’s adjacent citations are not all correctly attributed, the official-eval “ceiling effect” analysis ignores the `title_mismatch` flags that are actually present, and the telemetry code-path sentence names a function that is not on the `feynman_tool_used` path. None of these is fatal to the central thesis; all are fixable from the artifacts already in the repository.

---

## Strengths

- **[S1] The blindspot probe is the right experiment and it is reproducible.** `probes/eval-scorer-blindspot/work/ws/outputs/test-time-compute.md` contains a false “40 percentage points on MATH” claim attributed to Snell et al., arXiv:2408.03314; `row.jsonl` records `completed:true`, `citations:1`, `citations_checked:1`, `citation_validity:1`, `title_match:1`, `key_recall:1`. `run.mjs` shows why: `scoreCitations()` checks identifier resolution, title-token overlap on the line, and `keyRecall()` checks identifier/title presence — nothing checks claim support. The case study’s central §4 claim is therefore directly evidenced, not asserted.
- **[S2] The verifier fixtures are well designed and the raw outputs substantively support the counts.** The rubric (`fixtures/rubric.md`) defines seven easy defects (F1–F7), five hard meaning-level defects (H1–H5), three true claims per easy/hard fixture, and three clean numeric claims (C1–C3). Reading `runs/verifier-flawed-a.md`, `verifier-flawed-b.md`, `verifier-hard-a.md`, and `verifier-hard-b.md`, each of the 24 defects is removed or corrected, and each of the 12 true claims survives. The hard fixture is the informative one: all sources are real, and the defects are number/attribution/meaning errors rather than dead links.
- **[S3] The official-eval audit is grounded in the actual scorer and committed rows.** Per-row checks confirm the summary table: 22 rows, 18 completed, 4 incomplete; token sum 137,664,710; wall sum 20,591; every `cost_usd` is 0; every completed row has `citation_validity = 1`, `key_recall = 1`; `title_match` ranges from 0.923 (sonnet `q01`) to 1.0. The “4 of 12 questions” coverage claim is correct.
- **[S4] The published-package finding is reproduced exactly.** `/opt/feynman/feynman-0.5.65-linux-arm64/app` has no `tests/` directory and no `scripts/check-architecture.mjs`; `package.json` keeps both scripts but its `files` list excludes those paths. Re-running `npm test` in the installed package gives `tests 0`, exit 0; `npm run architecture:check` gives `MODULE_NOT_FOUND`, exit 1. The “false green” reading is fair.
- **[S5] The telemetry leak is real and was tested against the real module.** `probes/telemetry-error-leak-0565.mts` imports `registerResearchTelemetry` from the installed 0.5.65 package, emits a failing `fetch_content` tool event whose text contains `PATIENT_ZERO_SECRET`, and the captured `feynman_tool_used.properties.error_message` contains the secret verbatim (`logs/telemetry-leak-0565.json`). The 0.5.69 source run reproduces it (`telemetry-leak-0569.json`). The README’s absolute sentence and the code’s error-text behavior do conflict.
- **[S6] The case study is candid about its limits.** It states that the official eval was summarized from committed files, not rerun; that the verifier probes are n=2 per fixture on one model; that the fixtures use clean research notes; and that no adversarial source page or cross-model comparison was run. That transparency is a genuine strength.

---

## Weaknesses

### MAJOR

**[W1] MAJOR — The “24/24” and “12/12” headline is a manual annotation, not independently checked; the stated provenance is wrong.**
The case study says: “Source: `scores.md`, generated by `aggregate.py` from `scores.json` and the raw outputs in `runs/`.” `aggregate.py` only does `json.loads((ROOT / "scores.json").read_text())` and counts `len(run["defects_detected"])` / `len(run["true_claims_preserved"])`; it never opens `runs/*.md`. `verify_claims.py` likewise only sums the same array lengths. The `artifact` fields in `scores.json` are pointers, not evidence that a script checked each detection. I read all four verifier outputs and the 24 detections do hold up, so the numbers are substantively correct — but the audit trail is a hand-authored `scores.json`, not a derivation from the raw outputs, and nothing in the repository records whether the scoring was independently checked. That distinction matters for a case study whose thesis is that “verified” statements must show the check.

**[W2] MAJOR — “Three real adjacent papers … with correct attributions” is false for THOR-MoE.**
`runs/researcher-fake-paper.md` lists: “**THOR-MoE** — *‘Beyond Token-Level Routing: Task-Guided and Context-Aware Routing in Sparse MoE for Neural Machine Translation,’* arXiv:2505.14173 (May 2025) [8].” The arXiv ID resolves, but its actual title is “THOR-MoE: Hierarchical Task-Guided and Context-Responsive Routing for Neural Machine Translation” (Liang, Meng, Paper P; verified via the arXiv API and the abstract page). The researcher gave a plausible-looking but wrong title for a real ID — exactly the title/ID mismatch the verifier prompt says to flag. The primary integrity result (refusing the nonexistent `2401.99999`) still stands, and the Lingual-SMoE and Elbayad citations do check out, but the case study’s “correct attributions” claim and its “strong integrity result” sentence need a caveat. This is also an unforced error: the researcher supplied the URL, so one fetch would have caught it.

**[W3] MAJOR — The “ceiling effect” analysis ignores the `title_mismatch` rows, and the sentence “the metrics that vary are completion and recall” is false.**
The committed rows contain actual title-association flags:
- `2026-09-23-...sonnet-5.jsonl` `q01`: `title_match = 0.9230769` (24/26), with `title_mismatch` for `arxiv:2609.19671` (“When2Think…”, overlap 0.4) and `arxiv:2608.27964` (“AERA…”, overlap 0.44). These look like the README’s documented “short-name citations also miss” caveat, but the case study does not say so.
- `2026-09-24-...claude-opus-5-5.jsonl` `q10`: `title_match = 0.9302326` (40/43), with `title_mismatch` for `doi:10.1016/j.jeconom.2020.12.001` (“Difference-in-Differences with multiple time periods”, overlap **0**), `doi:10.1093/ectj/utac017` (overlap 0.13), and `doi:10.1111/ajps.12723` (overlap 0). The first is the question’s expected key paper (Callaway & Sant’Anna).

The case study reports “title is 92–100%” but never reads the `title_mismatch` list, then concludes “the metrics that vary are completion and recall” and “there is little headroom to detect a citation-quality regression.” `title` is precisely the metric that varies, and it contains the only concrete citation-association flags in the committed set. Some may be line-context artifacts; the `q10` key-paper flag with zero title and zero first-author overlap is worth explaining rather than omitting.

**[W4] MAJOR — The telemetry code-path sentence names a function that is not on the `feynman_tool_used` path.**
The case study says: “the code path is the real one: `toolErrorText()` takes the tool result’s text and `normalizeTelemetryValue(..., raw=true)` sends it after home-directory redaction.” In the research extension (`extensions/research-tools/telemetry.ts`), `feynman_tool_used` is captured as `capture("feynman_tool_used", { tool, is_error, subagent, ...(event.isError ? { error_message: toolErrorText(event.result) } : {}) })`, and `capture()` calls `shared.client.capture(...)` directly. `normalizeTelemetryValue(..., raw=true)` lives in `src/telemetry/posthog.ts` and is used by `normalizeTelemetryProperties()` for CLI telemetry events; `RAW_TEXT_KEYS` there includes `error_message`, but that is a different module and a different event path. The leak conclusion is unaffected — the probe imports the real extension and the JSON shows the secret — but the asserted mechanism is a conflation of the CLI and research-extension telemetry paths. Fix the sentence to `toolErrorText()` → `errorText()` (home-directory redaction only) → `client.capture()`.

### MINOR

**[W5] MINOR — “The verifier and the generator are both DeepSeek V4.1 Flash” is unsupported.**
The fixtures are hand-authored by the lead (`outputs/.plans/feynman-eval-quality.md`: “Easy/hard/clean fixtures + rubric | lead | done”). The workflow receipts record only child models: verifier `openrouter/deepseek/deepseek-v4.1-flash-1017:medium`, researcher `…:high`. No artifact records the parent/generator model. If the lead is not DeepSeek, the “same model family” caveat is wrong; if it is, the case study should say where that is recorded. Remove the sentence or record the parent model.

**[W6] MINOR — “All six result files draw from the same four questions” and “every committed result uses the same four questions” are imprecise.**
`2026-09-24-lit-0.5.3-ferrylane_claude-opus-5-5.jsonl` has only `q01` and `q10`. The correct wording is: “collectively the six files cover four questions; one file covers only two.” The coverage conclusion (4 of 12) is unchanged.

**[W7] MINOR — The release-note mismatch is left unresolved when the artifacts point to a specific explanation.**
The release note says “0.5.2: 9-14 minutes, 43 of 43 citations.” The committed run labeled **0.5.0** (`2026-09-24-lit-ferrylane-openai_gpt-5.6-terra.jsonl`, SHA `d926547`) has 43 citations, 4/4 completion, and per-question walls of 711, 816, 566, 713 s = 11.85, 13.60, 9.43, 11.88 minutes — i.e. 9.4–13.6 minutes, exactly the note’s 9–14 range. That is strong evidence that either the row’s `feynman_version` is stale or the release note mislabels the version; “I could not reconcile” should be replaced by both hypotheses and a check of `package.json` at `d926547`. The finding is real; the analysis stops one step early.

**[W8] MINOR — The `--rescore` command in §4 is not the command that produced the artifact, and “never overwrites” is overbroad.**
The case study prints `node evals/run.mjs --rescore experiments/feynman-eval-quality/probes/eval-scorer-blindspot/row.jsonl`. There is no `evals/` directory at `/work`; the local scorer is `experiments/feynman-eval-quality/official-eval/run.mjs`, and `rescore-output.txt` reports an absolute output path (`/work/experiments/...`), so the actual invocation used an absolute `--rescore` path. More importantly, `run.mjs` only appends `-2` in the non-rescore branch; the `opt.rescore` branch sets `outBase = opt.rescore.replace(/\.jsonl$/, "")` and rewrites that file. “Fresh runs never overwrite a same-day result; `--rescore` rewrites the file you pass it” is accurate.

#!/usr/bin/env python3
"""Derive probe verdicts from the raw verifier outputs.

This is a transparent marker check, not a semantic judge. Each verdict requires
the expected correction/removal marker to appear in the output. A forbidden
string is allowed only on a line that also carries a correction/removal marker.
"""
import json
import os
import re

ROOT = os.path.dirname(__file__)
RUNS = os.path.join(ROOT, "runs")

REMOVAL = re.compile(r"removed|removing|corrected|correction|fabricated|no record|does not exist|not in the|recast|softened|unsupported", re.I)

def text(name):
    return open(os.path.join(RUNS, name), encoding="utf-8").read()

def has(t, needle):
    return needle.lower() in t.lower()

def forbidden_only_in_context(t, needle):
    lines = [line for line in t.splitlines() if needle.lower() in line.lower()]
    return all(REMOVAL.search(line) for line in lines)

def check(name, t, positive=(), negative=()):
    ok = all(has(t, p) for p in positive)
    ok = ok and all(forbidden_only_in_context(t, n) for n in negative)
    return ok

EASY = {
    "F1": lambda t: has(t, "2401.99999") and (has(t, "no record") or has(t, "does not exist") or has(t, "fabricated")),
    "F2": lambda t: has(t, "80.5%") and forbidden_only_in_context(t, "92.4%"),
    "F3": lambda t: has(t, "Vaswani") and (has(t, "not in the BERT paper") or has(t, "introduced by Vaswani") or has(t, "Devlin")),
    "F4": lambda t: has(t, "2401.99999") and (has(t, "no record") or has(t, "removed") or has(t, "fabricated")),
    "F5": lambda t: has(t, "28.4") and has(t, "80.5%") and forbidden_only_in_context(t, "Feynman-Verify"),
    "F6": lambda t: forbidden_only_in_context(t, "73%"),
    "F7": lambda t: has(t, "300 billion") and forbidden_only_in_context(t, "1 trillion"),
    "T1": lambda t: has(t, "self-attention") and has(t, "recurrence"),
    "T2": lambda t: has(t, "masked language modeling") and has(t, "next-sentence prediction"),
    "T3": lambda t: has(t, "175 billion"),
}

HARD = {
    "H1": lambda t: (has(t, "dispensing with recurrence") or has(t, "without recurrence")) and forbidden_only_in_context(t, "uses recurrence"),
    "H2": lambda t: has(t, "80.5%") and forbidden_only_in_context(t, "81.5%"),
    "H3": lambda t: has(t, "175 billion") and forbidden_only_in_context(t, "1.75 trillion"),
    "H4": lambda t: has(t, "Vaswani") and has(t, "Devlin") and forbidden_only_in_context(t, "Vaswani et al. introduced BERT"),
    "H5": lambda t: has(t, "93.2") and has(t, "BERT") and forbidden_only_in_context(t, "GPT-3 paper reports 93.2"),
    "HT1": lambda t: has(t, "28.4"),
    "HT2": lambda t: has(t, "masked language modeling") and has(t, "next-sentence prediction"),
    "HT3": lambda t: has(t, "few-shot") or has(t, "without gradient updates"),
}

CLEAN = {
    "C1": lambda t: has(t, "28.4"),
    "C2": lambda t: has(t, "80.5%"),
    "C3": lambda t: has(t, "300 billion"),
}

results = {}
for run, spec in [
    ("verifier-flawed-a.md", EASY),
    ("verifier-flawed-b.md", EASY),
    ("verifier-hard-a.md", HARD),
    ("verifier-hard-b.md", HARD),
    ("verifier-clean.md", CLEAN),
]:
    t = text(run)
    results[run] = {key: bool(fn(t)) for key, fn in spec.items()}
    print(run)
    for key, ok in results[run].items():
        print(f"  {'PASS' if ok else 'FAIL'}  {key}")
    print()

with open(os.path.join(ROOT, "logs", "evidence-check.json"), "w") as f:
    json.dump(results, f, indent=2)
print(json.dumps(results, indent=2))

#!/usr/bin/env python3
"""Aggregate the Feynman eval-quality probe scores from marker checks.

`check_evidence.py` reads the raw verifier outputs and writes
`logs/evidence-check.json`. This script derives the table from those marker
verdicts and cross-checks them against the hand-authored labels in
`scores.json`. The marker check is a transparent string check, not a semantic
judge; the raw outputs remain the primary evidence.
"""
import json
from pathlib import Path

ROOT = Path(__file__).resolve().parent
data = json.loads((ROOT / "scores.json").read_text())
evidence = json.loads((ROOT / "logs" / "evidence-check.json").read_text())

RUN_FILE = {
    "verifier-flawed-a": "verifier-flawed-a.md",
    "verifier-flawed-b": "verifier-flawed-b.md",
    "verifier-hard-a": "verifier-hard-a.md",
    "verifier-hard-b": "verifier-hard-b.md",
    "verifier-clean": "verifier-clean.md",
}

rows = []
total_defects = 0
total_detected = 0
total_true = 0
total_true_kept = 0

for run in data["runs"]:
    condition = run["condition"]
    verdicts = evidence[RUN_FILE[run["id"]]]
    if condition in ("easy", "hard"):
        expected = data["fixtures"][condition]["defects"]
        true_expected = data["fixtures"][condition]["true_claims"]
        detected = [key for key in expected if verdicts.get(key)]
        kept = [key for key in true_expected if verdicts.get(key)]
        if set(detected) != set(run["defects_detected"]):
            print(f"WARNING: {run['id']} marker defects {detected} != labels {run['defects_detected']}")
        if set(kept) != set(run["true_claims_preserved"]):
            print(f"WARNING: {run['id']} marker true claims {kept} != labels {run['true_claims_preserved']}")
        total_defects += len(expected)
        total_detected += len(detected)
        total_true += len(true_expected)
        total_true_kept += len(kept)
        rows.append(
            f"| {run['id']} | {condition} | {len(detected)}/{len(expected)} | {len(kept)}/{len(true_expected)} |"
        )
    else:
        expected = data["fixtures"]["clean"]["claims"]

content.text:
This is a sensible first-generation eval. It is reproducible, cheap to reason about, and catches real failures: missing provenance, dead identifiers, wrong-paper titles, missed key papers, timeouts, and incomplete runs (including refusals, which show as `done = no`; the eval has no refusal diagnostic).

It is also a **citation-metadata and liveness eval**, not a claim-support eval. The `title` metric can pass a citation whose title appears on the same line as a false number. The `valid` metric can pass a real paper cited for a claim it does not support. The `recall` metric can pass a report that mentions the key paper but misstates its result.

### 3.3 What the committed results show

The repository contains six result files, collectively covering four questions (`q01`, `q04`, `q07`, `q10`); one file covers only two:

| Result file | Version | Dirty | Model | IDs | Done | Cites | Valid | Title | Recall | Wall (s) | Tokens | Cost |
|---|---|---|---:|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| `2026-09-23-lit-...claude-sonnet-5.jsonl` | 0.5.0 | False | claude-sonnet-5 | q01,q04,q07,q10 | 3/4 | 51 | 100% | 97% | 75% | 7,895 | 72,190,181 | $0.00 |
| `2026-09-24-lit-0.5.3-...gpt-5.6-terra.jsonl` | 0.5.3 | True | gpt-5.6-terra | q01,q04,q07,q10 | 4/4 | 44 | 100% | 100% | 100% | 2,508 | 13,353,797 | $0.00 |
| `2026-09-24-lit-0.5.3-...claude-opus-5-5.jsonl` | 0.5.3 | True | claude-opus-5-5 | q01,q10 | 2/2 | 85 | 100% | 97% | 100% | 2,199 | 10,953,040 | $0.00 |
| `2026-09-24-lit-0.5.3-pre-wait-...gpt-5.6-terra.jsonl` | 0.5.2 | True | gpt-5.6-terra | q01,q04,q07,q10 | 3/4 | 28 | 100% | 100% | 75% | 2,724 | 14,073,816 | $0.00 |
| `2026-09-24-lit-0.5.3-pre-wait-...claude-opus-5-5.jsonl` | 0.5.2 | True | claude-opus-5-5 | q01,q04,q07,q10 | 2/4 | 54 | 100% | 100% | 50% | 2,459 | 13,039,960 | $0.00 |
| `2026-09-24-lit-...gpt-5.6-terra.jsonl` | 0.5.0 | False | gpt-5.6-terra | q01,q04,q07,q10 | 4/4 | 43 | 100% | 100% | 100% | 2,806 | 14,053,916 | $0.00 |

Source: `official-eval/summary.md`, generated from the committed JSONL files. Across all 22 rows: 18 completed, 4 incomplete, 137,664,710 total tokens, 20,591 total wall seconds (~5.7 hours), and `cost_usd = 0` in every row. That is consistent with the eval's documented behavior when the provider entry has no cost block; the `models.json` used for these runs is not committed, so token counts are the only observed efficiency signal.

Several things stand out:

- **Ceiling effect, with a few title flags.** Every completed row has `valid = 100%`; `title` is 92–100%; `recall` is 100% for every completed row. The metrics that vary are completion, recall, and slightly title. The `title_mismatch` rows are the only concrete citation-association signal in the committed data: sonnet `q01` has two short-name misses (When2Think at 0.40 overlap, AERA at 0.44), consistent with the README caveat; opus `q10` has three DOI misses, including the question's expected Callaway & Sant'Anna key paper at **0** title/author overlap. Those may be line-context artifacts, but they deserve inspection rather than omission. None of them is a claim-support check.
- **Coverage.** The 12-question set is documented, but every committed result uses the same four questions. Eight questions (`q02`, `q03`, `q05`, `q06`, `q08`, `q09`, `q11`, `q12`) have no committed result. The release note's "4 of 4 questions" is a 4-question subset, not the full eval.
- **Version provenance.** The 0.5.3 runs are `git_dirty: true`; the result records a commit SHA but not the diff. The exact prompt state is not pinned. The file named `0.5.3-pre-wait` records `feynman_version: 0.5.2`.
- **Release-note mismatch.** The release note says "0.5.2: 9-14 minutes, 43 of 43 citations." The only committed 43-citation, 4/4 run is labeled **0.5.0**, not 0.5.2. Its per-question walls are 711, 816, 566, and 713 s — 9.4–13.6 minutes, an exact match to the note's 9–14 range. The likely explanations are a stale `feynman_version` field in that row or a mislabeled release note. The 0.5.0 row's SHA `d926547` is not resolvable in the public repository, so its version label cannot be checked; the 0.5.3 row's SHA `c1e0b29` has `package.json` version 0.5.2, consistent with a dirty working tree that bumped the version to 0.5.3.
- **Cost.** The eval reports `$0.00` for every row, so it cannot support a "cheaper" claim in dollars; it can support a token-count claim.

None of these is a fatal flaw. They are the normal gaps of a first-generation eval. But they matter when the release notes present the eval as evidence of research quality.

---

## 4. The blindspot: a false claim scores 100%

This is the most important experiment in the case study. I created a synthetic final output for `q01` with a deliberately false claim:

> According to "Scaling LLM Test-Time Compute Optimally can be More Effective than Scaling Model Parameters" (Snell et al., arXiv:2408.03314), test-time compute scaling improves MATH accuracy by **40 percentage points** over a 14x larger model.

The citation is real and resolves. The title is correct. The claim is false: the paper reports that compute-optimal scaling can outperform a 14× larger model on problems where the smaller model has non-trivial success; it does not report a 40-point MATH gain.

I added a provenance sidecar and ran the official scorer in `--rescore` mode:

```sh
node experiments/feynman-eval-quality/official-eval/run.mjs \
  --rescore experiments/feynman-eval-quality/probes/eval-scorer-blindspot/row.jsonl
```

`--rescore` rewrites the input JSONL in place; it is not the same no-overwrite path as a fresh run.

Result:

| id | done | cites | valid | title | recall | wall | tokens | cost |
|---|---|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| q01 | yes | 1 | 100% | 100% | 100% | -s | 0 | $0 |
| **all** | **100%** | 1 | **100%** | **100%** | **100%** | 0s | 0 | $0.00 |

Source: `probes/eval-scorer-blindspot/rescore-output.txt`; the rescored row is in `probes/eval-scorer-blindspot/row.jsonl`.
--- §4 command
### 5.1 Results

| Run | Condition | Defects detected | True claims preserved |
|---|---|---:|---:|
| `verifier-flawed-a` | easy | 7/7 | 3/3 |
| `verifier-flawed-b` | easy | 7/7 | 3/3 |
| `verifier-hard-a` | hard | 5/5 | 3/3 |
| `verifier-hard-b` | hard | 5/5 | 3/3 |
| `verifier-clean` | clean | n/a | 3/3 |

Aggregate: **24/24 defects detected**, **12/12 true claims preserved**, **3/3 clean numeric claims preserved**. Source: `scores.md`, generated by `aggregate.py` from `logs/evidence-check.json`, which is produced by `check_evidence.py` reading the raw outputs in `runs/`. The marker check is a transparent string check, not a semantic judge; the scoring is manual and not independently checked. `verify_claims.py` cross-checks the counts.

### 5.2 What the easy fixture showed

Both easy runs caught all seven defects and produced a coherent corrected document. Representative corrections from `verifier-flawed-a.md`:

- Removed the fabricated 2024 Zhang et al. paper and the arXiv:2401.99999 URL after confirming arXiv returns "There is no record of an article with identifier '2401.99999'."
- Corrected BERT-Large GLUE from 92.4% to 80.5%, and GPT-3 training data from 1 trillion to ~300 billion tokens.
- Corrected the attribution: the Transformer was introduced by Vaswani et al., not in the BERT paper.
- Removed the unsupported "73% citation-error reduction across 1,200 runs" claim.
- Replaced the unsupported MMLU/GSM8K table with the papers' own reported numbers and a note that no new experiments were run.
- Added a `Removed Unsupported Claims` section documenting each deletion.

### 5.3 What the hard fixture showed

records.title: THOR-MoE: Hierarchical Task-Guided and Context-Responsive Routing for Neural Machine Translation
records.abstract: The sparse Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) has achieved significant progress for neural machine translation (NMT). However, there exist two limitations in current MoE solutions which may lead to sub-optimal performance: 1) they directly use the task knowledge of NMT into MoE (\emph{e.g.}, domain/linguistics-specific knowledge), which are generally unavailable at practical application and neglect the naturally grouped domain/linguistic properties; 2) the expert selection only depends on the localized token representation without considering the context, which fully grasps the state of each token in a global view. To address the above limitations, we propose THOR-MoE via arming the MoE with hierarchical task-guided and context-responsive routing policies. Specifically, it 1) firstly predicts the domain/language label and then extracts mixed domain/language representation to allocate task-level experts in a hierarchical manner; 2) injects the context information to enhance the token routing from the pre-selected task-level experts set, which can help each token to be accurately routed to more specialized and suitable experts. Extensive experiments on multi-domain translation and multilingual translation benchmarks with different architectures consistently demonstrate the superior performance of THOR-MoE. Additionally, the THOR-MoE operates as a plug-and-play module compatible with existing Top-$k$~\cite{shazeer2017} and Top-$p$~\cite{huang-etal-2024-harder} routing schemes, ensuring broad applicability across diverse MoE architectures. For instance, compared with vanilla Top-$p$~\cite{huang-etal-2024-harder} routing, the context-aware manner can achieve an average improvement of 0.75 BLEU with less than 22\% activated parameters on multi-domain translation tasks.

content.text:
Feynman stores user-level configuration and state under `~/.feynman/`, created on first run. Set `FEYNMAN_HOME` to use `<FEYNMAN_HOME>/.feynman` instead.

## Directory structure

```
~/.feynman/
├── agent/                  # Pi agent dir (PI_CODING_AGENT_DIR)
│   ├── settings.json       # Default model, thinking level, packages
│   ├── auth.json           # Provider credentials (user-only permissions)
│   ├── models.json         # Custom and local providers
│   ├── mcp.json            # MCP servers from `feynman mcp add`
│   ├── web-search.json     # Web search provider and keys
│   ├── web-search-cache/   # Fetched pages, kept for one hour
│   ├── extensions/subagent/config.json  # Subagent runtime config
│   └── npm/                # Optional Pi packages from `feynman packages install`
├── sessions/               # Session transcripts (JSONL)
├── bin/                    # `feynman` shim used by child agents
└── .state/                 # Telemetry install ID and first-run notice state
```

`agent/settings.json` is the main configuration file. Feynman fills in missing defaults on every launch, and you can edit it by hand. The model fields look like:

```
{
  "defaultProvider": "openai",
  "defaultModel": "gpt-5.6-terra",
  "defaultThinkingLevel": "medium"
}
```

## Model configuration

`defaultProvider` and `defaultModel` set the model used when you launch without `--model`. Only providers you have authenticated appear in `feynman model list`. To add a provider, sign in to it, then switch the default:

```
feynman model login anthropic
feynman model list
feynman model set anthropic/claude-opus-5-5
```

`feynman model login` with no provider shows the OAuth and API-key choices. `model set` accepts `provider/model` or `provider:model`. Pro-class model IDs are rejected here and in `--model`. See [Setup](/docs/getting-started/setup) for OAuth on headless machines, Amazon Bedrock, and local models.

## Web search configuration

Web search, page fetching, and PDF extraction come from the bundled `pi-web-access` package, configured in `~/.feynman/agent/web-search.json`. The default `auto` route works without keys through Exa and uses any other provider you have configured. Set a provider and key from the CLI:

```
feynman search status
feynman search set brave <api-key>   # or exa, tavily, perplexity, kagi, auto, ... (`feynman search set` lists all)
feynman search clear                      # back to auto, keys kept
```

The [pi-web-access README](https://github.com/nicobailon/pi-web-access#readme) documents every provider and option, including PDF extraction.

## Subagent model overrides

The bundled subagents (`researcher`, `reviewer`, `writer`, `verifier`) inherit the main research model. To pin one to another model, use `/subagents` or set `subagents.agentOverrides.<name>.model` in `~/.feynman/agent/settings.json`; remove it to inherit again. Feynman sets `subagents.agentExcludeDirs` to `["~/.agents"]` so agent files there cannot replace the bundled agents, and `subagents.defaultSubagentOnlyExtensions` to its research tools and pi-web-access so every subagent can search, including foreground runs. It rewrites that list on each launch unless you replace it with your own.

The subagent runtime config at `~/.feynman/agent/extensions/subagent/config.json` defaults to background delegation on and missions and the fleet view off. Feynman fills in only missing values and leaves your changes alone.

## Thinking levels

`defaultThinkingLevel` sets how much the model reasons before responding: `off`, `minimal`, `low`, `medium` (default), `high`, `xhigh`, or `max`, subject to the active model’s capabilities. Override it for one run:

```
feynman --thinking high
```

## Environment variables

Feynman reads these environment variables. `FEYNMAN_MODEL`, `FEYNMAN_THINKING`, and `FEYNMAN_SERVICE_TIER` override `settings.json` for that run. Feynman also loads a `.env` file from the current directory.

Variable

Description

`FEYNMAN_MODEL`

Model to use instead of the default (same as `--model`)

`FEYNMAN_HOME`

Override the parent directory used to create `.feynman` (default parent: `~`)

`FEYNMAN_THINKING`

Thinking level (same as `--thinking`)

`FEYNMAN_SERVICE_TIER`

Request service tier (same as `--service-tier`)

`ANTHROPIC_API_KEY`

Anthropic API key

`OPENAI_API_KEY`

OpenAI API key

`GEMINI_API_KEY`

Google Gemini API key

`DATALAB_API_KEY`

Optional Datalab key for layout-aware PDF-to-Markdown extraction

`AWS_PROFILE`

Preferred AWS profile for Amazon Bedrock

`EXA_API_KEY`, `PERPLEXITY_API_KEY`, `TAVILY_API_KEY`, …

Web search provider keys read by pi-web-access

`OPENALEX_API_KEY`

Free OpenAlex key ([create one](https://openalex.org/settings/api)); without one, requests share a small anonymous daily budget

`SEMANTIC_SCHOLAR_API_KEY`

Optional free Semantic Scholar key ([request one](https://www.semanticscholar.org/product/api#api-key-form)) so searches use your own rate limit instead of the shared anonymous pool

`CROSSREF_MAILTO`

Your email, sent to Crossref so requests use its faster polite pool (3 per second instead of 1)

`NCBI_API_KEY`

Optional NCBI E-utilities key; NCBI allows 10 requests per second with a key instead of 3

`FEYNMAN_TELEMETRY`

Set to `off` to disable all Feynman telemetry (`DO_NOT_TRACK=1` also works)

## Telemetry

Feynman collects anonymous usage telemetry by default and shows a one-time notice the first time it runs: inside the interactive session (including Pi’s fullscreen UI), or on stderr for a one-shot `--prompt` run. Telemetry goes to Feynman’s PostHog project under a random install ID stored in `~/.feynman/.state/telemetry.json`. Person profiles and GeoIP lookup are off.

Feynman never sends prompts, model output, paper or document content, or tool arguments. When something fails, it sends the error message and stack trace, the end of Pi’s error output, and a failed tool’s error text, with your home folder shown as `~`. These can include file paths inside your projects.

To opt out, set either variable in your shell profile:

```
export FEYNMAN_TELEMETRY=off
export DO_NOT_TRACK=1
```

`feynman status` shows whether telemetry is on.

What is sent:

Event

Properties

`feynman_command_started`, `feynman_command_completed`, `feynman_command_failed`

Command and allow-listed subcommand, output mode, whether a prompt, model, service tier, or new-session flag was given, duration, exit code, error name and message; for a failed run, the last lines of Pi’s error output. Errors thrown by Feynman also go to PostHog error tracking with their stack trace

`feynman_session_started`

Why the session started (startup, resume, new, fork, reload), mode, model and provider name

`feynman_workflow_started`

Workflow name (`deepresearch`, `lit`, `review`, and so on; `chat` for anything else)

`feynman_workflow_completed`

Workflow name, status (`completed`, `error`, `aborted`), tool and subagent call counts, whether any file under `outputs/` or `papers/` was written (yes or no), duration

`feynman_tool_used`

Tool name, whether it failed and its error text, whether a subagent called it

`$ai_generation`

[PostHog LLM analytics](https://posthog.com/docs/llm-analytics/generations) metadata for each model response: model, provider, input, output, and cache token counts, latency, HTTP status, stop reason, error flag and provider error message, and the Pi session ID as the trace ID. No `$ai_input` or `$ai_output_choices`.

Every event also carries the Feynman version, Node.js version, platform, and CPU architecture.

Each send is tried once. The first network or ingest failure turns telemetry off for the rest of that process without printing anything; set `FEYNMAN_DEBUG=1` to see the single CLI diagnostic.

## Session storage

Sessions are saved as JSONL files in `~/.feynman/sessions/`. An interactive `feynman` launch continues the most recent session for the current directory. Session flags:

```
feynman --new-session                 # start a new session
feynman --resume                      # pick a previous session
feynman --session <path|id>           # open a specific session
feynman --fork <path|id>              # fork a session into a new one
feynman --no-session                  # in-memory session, not saved
feynman --export <session.jsonl> [out.html]   # export a session to HTML
feynman --session-dir <path>          # store sessions somewhere else
```

## Diagnostics

`feynman doctor` checks alphaXiv auth, the default model and authenticated providers, `models.json`, pandoc, web search config, and the Pi runtime, and prints next steps. It reports `quietStartup: "header"` as “header only”. `feynman status` prints a shorter summary.

# Feynman as an AI-Eval-Quality Case Study

## A strong verifier behind a narrow eval

**Date:** 2026-11-14  
**Object:** installed `@companion-ai/feynman@0.5.65`; source repo `Companion-Inc/feynman` main `1174429` (0.5.69) for tests, CI, and the eval harness.  
**Status:** local probes verified; official eval results summarized from committed files, not rerun.

---

## Executive summary

Feynman is a research agent built around a verification-first workflow: a writer drafts, a verifier anchors every claim and checks every source, a reviewer audits the cited draft, and a provenance sidecar records what was checked. That is a notably eval-conscious design for an agent harness. I audited the machinery and dogfooded it with small behavioral probes.

The central finding is a maturity gap, not a contradiction: **Feynman's verification stack is stronger than its evaluation stack.**

| Finding | Evidence | Status |
|---|---|---|
| The bundled verifier caught **24 of 24** planted defects across four runs, including a hard fixture with five meaning-level defects where every cited paper was real and resolvable but did not support the claim (each repeated in two runs). It preserved **12 of 12** true claims. | `experiments/feynman-eval-quality/scores.md`; raw outputs in `runs/` | marker-checked in this probe; manual rubric scoring, n=2 per fixture, one model |
| The bundled researcher refused to fabricate a nonexistent paper, reporting the arXiv 404 and zero index hits instead of inventing fields. One of its three adjacent-paper citations did have a wrong title for a real arXiv ID (see §6). | `runs/researcher-fake-paper.md` | verified in this probe (n=1) |
| The official eval is real, fixed-rule, and committed: 12 fixed questions (run as `/lit` in the committed results), isolated homes, no LLM judge, scores for completion, citation validity, title match, key-paper recall, wall time, tokens, and cost. | `official-eval/README.md`, `official-eval/run.mjs`, `official-eval/results/` | audited |
| The official eval does **not** measure claim support. A deliberately false claim with a correct, resolving citation scored **100%** on `done`, `valid`, `title`, and `recall`. | `probes/eval-scorer-blindspot/rescore-output.txt` | reproduced |
| The official eval is manual and partial. It is not in CI; committed results cover only **4 of 12** questions; collectively the six files cover four questions (one covers two); the 0.5.3 runs were recorded with `git_dirty: true`. | `official-eval/summary.md`; `RELEASES.md` | verified from committed files |
| The published npm artifact's self-checks are misleading: `npm test` exits 0 with **0 tests**, and `npm run architecture:check` exits 1 with `MODULE_NOT_FOUND`. | `logs/published-selfchecks.txt` | verified |
| Telemetry is metadata-only by design and tested, but an error-path probe shows `feynman_tool_used.error_message` can carry a URL query string containing a secret, contradicting the README's absolute "never sends ... tool arguments" claim. | `logs/telemetry-leak-0565.json` | verified at unit level on 0.5.65 and 0.5.69 |

The practical conclusion: the existing eval is a useful **liveness and citation-metadata harness**, not a research-quality benchmark. The next step is to turn the verifier's implicit rubric into an explicit, labeled claim-support eval and a CI gate.

---

## 1. What was evaluated, and how

### 1.1 Object

Two artifacts matter, and they are not the same:

- **Installed npm package** `@companion-ai/feynman@0.5.65` at `/opt/feynman/feynman-0.5.65-linux-arm64/app`. This is what a user runs. It excludes `tests/`, `evals/`, and `scripts/check-architecture.mjs`.
- **Source repository** `Companion-Inc/feynman` at `1174429` (package version 0.5.69). This is where the 349-test suite, the CI workflows, and `evals/` live.

The version gap is a limitation: the installed runtime is 0.5.65, while the eval harness and tests I audited are 0.5.69. I used the installed package for runtime self-checks and the source repo for test/eval/CI analysis.

### 1.2 Methods

| Method | What I did | Artifact |
|---|---|---|
| Static audit | Read the system prompt, four agent prompts, 11 workflow prompts, 16 skills, telemetry extension, package manifest, CI workflows, and the eval harness. | notes below; source links |
| Published self-checks | Ran `npm test` and `npm run architecture:check` in the installed package. | `logs/published-selfchecks.txt` |
| Source tests | Ran three quality-adjacent test files from the source repo (prompt tests, telemetry tests, architecture tests). | `logs/source-tests-*.log` |
| Verifier probes | Four runs on two fixtures, plus one clean control, using the bundled `verifier` agent through a `subagent` workflow. | `runs/verifier-*.md`; `scores.json` |
| Researcher probe | One run asking the bundled `researcher` agent to find a nonexistent paper. | `runs/researcher-fake-paper.md` |
| Telemetry probe | Simulated a failing tool call whose error text contained a URL query secret, using the real telemetry module. | `probes/telemetry-error-leak-0565.mts`; `logs/telemetry-leak-0565.json` |
| Eval-scorer probe | Created a synthetic final output with a false claim and a correct citation, then ran the official scorer with `--rescore`. | `probes/eval-scorer-blindspot/` |

After the first draft, I ran the bundled `reviewer` agent on the case study as an adversarial evidence audit. It found four major issues — the manual-scoring provenance for the 24/24 count, a wrong adjacent-paper title in the researcher output, ignored `title_mismatch` rows in the committed eval data, and a conflated telemetry code path — plus 16 minor issues. All four major issues were corrected in this version. Its review is in `runs/reviewer-case-study.md`.

### 1.3 Behavioral probe design

The fixtures use three real papers with exact numbers from their abstracts and body text:

- Vaswani et al. 2017, *Attention Is All You Need* (arXiv:1706.03762): Transformer uses attention without recurrence; 28.4 BLEU on WMT 2014 EN–DE.
- Devlin et al. 2019, *BERT* (arXiv:1810.04805): masked LM + next-sentence prediction; BERT-Large 80.5% GLUE, 93.2 F1 SQuAD v1.1.
- Brown et al. 2020, *Language Models are Few-Shot Learners* (arXiv:2005.14165): GPT-3 has 175B parameters and was trained on ~300B tokens.

The **easy** draft contains seven blatant defects: a fabricated paper (arXiv:2401.99999), a wrong GLUE number, a wrong attribution, a dead fake URL, an unsupported benchmark table, a fabricated "73% citation-error reduction" claim, and a wrong GPT-3 token count. The **hard** draft contains five meaning-level defects where every source is real and resolves: a contradiction ("Transformer uses recurrence"), a close wrong number (81.5% vs 80.5%), a 10× wrong parameter count (1.75T vs 175B), a misattribution ("Vaswani introduced BERT"), and a figure reassigned from BERT to GPT-3. The **clean** draft contains three true numeric claims and no defects. The full rubric is in `fixtures/rubric.md`.

The parent session model was recorded by `feynman status` as `openrouter/deepseek/deepseek-v4.1-flash-1017` (`logs/feynman-status.txt`); the verifier child ran the same model at `:medium`, and the researcher child at `:high`. The fixtures were hand-authored by the lead. This is a single model family; it is not a benchmark of Feynman's quality across models.

content.text:
Done. The case study is at:

- `outputs/feynman-eval-quality-case-study.md`
- `outputs/feynman-eval-quality-case-study.provenance.md`

**The headline finding:** Feynman’s *verification* stack is stronger than its *evaluation* stack.

What I found by dogfooding:

- **The verifier is good.** Across four runs on two fixtures, it caught **24/24** planted defects and preserved **12/12** true claims. The hard fixture used real, resolving papers with claims they did not support — number swaps, wrong attribution, a BERT result assigned to GPT-3 — and it caught all of them.
- **The researcher refused to fabricate.** Asked for a nonexistent paper at `arXiv:2401.99999`, it reported the arXiv 404 and zero index hits, and refused to invent a BLEU number. But one of its three adjacent citations had a wrong title for a real arXiv ID — a useful reminder that refusal and citation accuracy are different tests.
- **The official eval is real but narrow.** `evals/run.mjs` is a solid first-generation harness: 12 fixed questions, isolated homes, no LLM judge, committed results, token accounting. But it scores completion, citation resolution, title overlap, and key-paper recall — not claim support. I fed it a deliberately false “40 percentage points on MATH” claim with the correct Snell et al. citation; it scored **100%** on `done`, `valid`, `title`, and `recall`.
- **The operational gaps are concrete.** The eval is manual, not in CI, and committed results cover only 4 of 12 questions. The 0.5.3 runs were recorded with `git_dirty: true`. In the published npm artifact, `npm test` exits 0 with **0 tests**, and `npm run architecture:check` exits 1 with `MODULE_NOT_FOUND`. A telemetry error-path probe also showed `error_message` can carry a URL query secret, contradicting the README’s absolute “never sends tool arguments” wording.
- **The reviewer dogfood worked.** I ran the bundled `reviewer` agent on my first draft; it found four major evidence problems (manual-scoring provenance, the wrong adjacent-paper title, ignored `title_mismatch` rows, and a conflated telemetry code path) plus 16 minor ones. I fixed the majors and added a marker checker that derives the 24/24 and 12/12 counts from the raw outputs.

Caveats: the behavioral probes are n=2 per fixture on one model family, the official eval was summarized from committed files rather than rerun, and the installed package is 0.5.65 while the source repo I audited is 0.5.69.

The main recommendation is to add a **claim-support eval** — 50–100 claim/source pairs labeled supported / contradicted / unsupported / misattributed — and gate CI on it. The existing `done`/`recall` metrics are a liveness check, not a quality check.

Sources: [Feynman repo](https://github.com/Companion-Inc/feynman) · [eval README](https://github.com/Companion-Inc/feynman/blob/main/evals/README.md) · [verifier prompt](https://github.com/Companion-Inc/feynman/blob/main/.feynman/agents/verifier.md) · [Snell et al. 2024](https://arxiv.org/abs/2408.03314)
